summary: Describes procedures for VPLS provider edge routers to send multicast traffic only to ports with interested PIM routers or IGMP hosts. It uses PIM snooping, where PEs listen to control messages, or PIM proxying, where they generate their own Join/Prune messages.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of giving a copy of the show to everyone, you only give one to people who asked for it.

subtitle: How to efficiently deliver multicast content within virtual private networks by listening to routing requests.

tldr.problem: In virtual private networks that carry multicast traffic, copies are sent to every customer site even if nobody there wants to watch. This wastes bandwidth and network capacity.
tldr.mechanism: Provider routers listen to (snoop on) Protocol Independent Multicast control messages from customer routers to learn which sites have interested viewers. They then replicate traffic only to those sites, or generate their own routing requests (proxy) when customer routers suppress duplicates.
tldr.outcome: VPLS multicast becomes much more efficient. Only sites that requested the content receive it, reducing provider network load while maintaining compatibility with existing customer routing protocols.

facts.label: States tracked
facts.value: Per port, upstream neighbor, source, and group (Port, S, G, N)

today: RFC 8220 is an Informational RFC documenting how virtual private network provider edges can use PIM snooping and proxying to efficiently deliver multicast content. It builds on a strong foundation of existing PIM standards and is useful for service providers deploying VPLS with multicast support. The procedures remain relevant as providers continue to support multicast within virtualized networks.

sections.title: The Multicast Problem in Virtual Networks
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) makes distant customer sites appear as if they are connected to the same local area network (LAN). A VPLS Provider Edge (PE) router forwards frames based on learned MAC addresses, just like a switch.

For unicast frames to known addresses, the PE only forwards to the specific customer site that owns that address. But multicast frames—sent to a group address for distribution to many receivers—are treated as unknown traffic and flooded to all customer sites and remote PEs.

This creates two problems described in RFC 5501:

  1. Replication to non-members: Multicast traffic is sent to every site even if no one there wants to receive it.
  2. Wasted replication on shared paths: When multiple virtual connections share physical cables, the same traffic may be replicated multiple times unnecessarily.

This RFC solves problem 1 by having PE routers listen to Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) control messages, learning where interested receivers are located, so traffic goes only to sites that requested it.
sections.plainLanguage: A PE router is like a mail delivery office that initially sends every parcel to every house. But if it listens to customers saying 'I want sports magazines,' it can skip houses that said 'no thanks.'

sections.title: How PIM Snooping Works
sections.content:
Instead of fully participating in PIM routing, a VPLS PE router snoops on PIM messages—it listens to them without modifying how customers' routers communicate.

PIM Hello messages let the PE discover which customer routers (and thus which customer sites) exist. From Hello messages, the PE learns each router's IP address, which port (attachment circuit or pseudowire) it connects to, and capabilities like designated router priority and join suppression support.

PIM Join/Prune messages are how routers request (or stop requesting) multicast traffic. When a PE overhears a Join for a group (G) or a source-group pair (S,G), it knows that site is interested in that traffic. When it hears a Prune, that site is no longer interested.

The PE snoops on these messages, builds a state table of which sites want which multicast streams, and forwards data traffic only to ports where Joins were snooped. This happens transparently—the PE does not consume or modify the PIM messages; it just listens and learns.
sections.plainLanguage: The PE listens to customer routers saying 'I want the sports channel' and 'I don't want the cooking channel.' It remembers this and sends each channel only to sites that asked for it.

sections.title: Snooping, Relay, and Proxying
sections.content:
Three different approaches achieve this goal, with different tradeoffs:

PIM Snooping
The PE listens to PIM messages and floods them normally. It builds state from snooped messages but generates no new messages. Simplest to implement, truly transparent, but requires customer routers to disable Join suppression so the PE sees all Joins.
PIM Relay
The PE snoops on Join/Prune messages and forwards them only to specific upstream ports instead of flooding them. It does not generate new messages. Allows customer routers to use Join suppression, but adds some latency between a Join and traffic arriving.
PIM Proxying
The PE consumes Join/Prune messages and generates its own upstream Joins, aggregating requests from many customers into a single upstream request. Allows customer Join suppression, scales better with many customers, but loses transparency since the PE modifies control traffic.

The choice depends on whether customer routers support disabling Join suppression (use snooping if yes, proxying if no) and whether Join latency is a concern. Join suppression is an optimization where routers suppress sending duplicate Joins if they already heard another router on the LAN send one for the same group. If a PE snoops and only relays Join/Prune messages, it cannot see suppressed Joins, and sites with suppressed routers will not receive traffic. Proxying solves this by having the PE generate its own Joins.
sections.plainLanguage: The PE can listen quietly, forward messages carefully, or speak up and send its own requests upstream—three different ways to manage which customer sites get which channels.

sections.title: Building Multicast State from Join/Prune Messages
sections.content:
Protocol Independent Multicast comes in several variants. This RFC focuses on PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), which assumes multicast receivers are spread sparsely across the network and uses explicit Joins to build distribution trees.

When a PE snoops on PIM-SM, it builds a state table for each (source, group) or (group) combination on each customer attachment point, tracking whether a Join or Prune is active. The PE learns these states per upstream neighbor (N), which is the next-hop router in the snooped Join/Prune message. This is important because in some network topologies, multiple routers on a LAN might be upstream to different sources, and the PE must handle each separately.

The PE maintains timers for each state:

  • Expiry Timer (ET): Restarted each time a Join is received. If no Join is received within the hold time, the state expires and is removed.
  • Prune-Pending Timer (PPT): Started when a Prune is received, giving the upstream router a chance to send another Join to cancel the Prune. If the timer expires and no conflicting Join arrives, the state is pruned.

From these per-port, per-upstream-neighbor states, the PE computes which traffic to forward and to which ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The PE writes down for each customer site and each channel: 'site A joined channel 5, site B just left channel 3.' When the timer expires without a new Join, it forgets that interest.

sections.title: How Multicast Traffic Is Forwarded
sections.content:
Once the PE has built its snooped state, it forwards data traffic according to these rules:

  • Traffic arriving on a port is not sent back out that same port. This prevents loops.
  • Traffic from a pseudowire (remote PE connection) is never forwarded to other pseudowires. This respects VPLS split-horizon rules and prevents redundant replication.
  • For (S,G) traffic (source S, group G): Forward to all attachment circuits (AC, customer ports) where a Join(S,G) was snooped, and to all upstream neighbors that might be sources for competing traffic (to trigger PIM Assert elections so the best source is selected).
  • For (*,G) traffic (any source, group G): Forward to ACs with snooped Join(*,G) messages, plus upstream ports for Assert purposes.
  • If an upstream port has a snooped (S,G) state and a (*,G) state, use the more specific (S,G) state to decide whether to forward or prune on that port.

When multicast sources are directly connected to the VPLS (not behind a customer router that would send Joins), special handling is needed. The RFC recommends that multicast sources be placed behind routers so their traffic naturally triggers upstream Joins.
sections.plainLanguage: The PE sends the channel to every customer site that asked for it (Join), to the upstream routers (in case of conflicts), and not back to where it came from. If two sources send the same channel, the routers fight it out with Assert messages, and only the winner sends to each site.

sections.title: Other PIM Modes and Considerations
sections.content:
PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) is the focus of this RFC. PIM Source-Specific Multicast (PIM-SSM) is similar but only supports (S,G) Joins, not (*,G) Joins (group-wide, source-independent joins).

PIM Dense Mode (PIM-DM) uses a flood-and-prune approach opposite to PIM-SM. Traffic floods everywhere initially, then is pruned back from areas with no interest. PIM snooping works with PIM-DM as well, using similar state machines to handle Prune and Graft messages.

Bidirectional PIM (BIDIR-PIM) allows traffic to flow both toward and away from the source, enabling many-to-many applications. However, PIM snooping procedures may interfere with BIDIR-PIM's design, and further study is recommended before deploying snooping on BIDIR-PIM networks.

IGMP Snooping Interaction: IGMP snooping (RFC 4541) learns about multicast receivers (hosts) that join groups. When both IGMP and PIM snooping are enabled, a PE should use PIM-discovered routers to determine forwarding ports to LANs with routers, and IGMP-discovered hosts for other ports.
sections.plainLanguage: Different PIM modes work in different ways—some push traffic everywhere and then prune it back, others pull traffic explicitly. The PE needs to understand which mode is in use and handle it accordingly.
